Q: i don't understand boolean A:

The difference between = and ==

The single = is the assignment operator. Inside a condition in an if statement too.

your right, in my original code I had if (isLightOn = false) {

and that gave the "the light is off" output

if (isLightOn = false) assigns false to isLightOn and then evaluates to the assigned value, that is, false. So in this case the else part of your if-else statement is executed and the light is off is printed.

BTW your IDE ought to warn you that the value of isLightOn = false is always false rendering the if-else statement rather pointless

The ==, double equal sign, is the equality operator. It compares the two values (without modifying any) and evaluates to true if they are equal.

The preferred way

All of this said and repeating what others have said: Prefer if (isLightOn) even if it means reversing the two parts of your if-else statement. Or if you don’t want that, use the not operator or exclamation mark: if (! isLightOn) (the space after ! is optional and most don’t type it; I personally find the negation easier to spot when separated from the variable name).

Q: ARM Literal Pool definition in a mixed C and assembly function A:

Between back-to-back asm statements, at -O0 the compiler will typically only emit its own asm instructions as part of handling the input/output constraints, like loading a value into a register for an "r" constraint.

Your code has a C if between some of its statements, and all your asm is GNU C Basic Asm which isn't safely usable inside a (non-naked) function since you can't declare clobbers. (https://gcc.gnu.org/wiki/ConvertBasicAsmToExtended). If Basic Asm was usable, then your reasoning would be correct, but Extended asm using constraints can easily involve compiler-generated instructions. (e.g. to set up the address of a global var into a register if you use it as an input or output operand. Or maybe randomly wasting instructions at -O0 getting local vars in and out of registers.)

Equally importantly, if you're aiming for performance, disabling optimization will defeat the purpose and most of the possible benefit of mixing C with inline asm in most cases.

In another answer, you mentioned m68k and PIC and using hard registers. I assume you're talking about non-inline asm. You can write whole ARM functions in pure assembly, just following the standard calling convention. That's a lot easier to learn, and better documented. But that's not what you're asking about here, so the correct answer is super different.

Q: Deleting rows from 3 tables at once in PHP A:

I haven't tried it, but you could try multi-table deletes:

http://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/5.6/en/delete.html#id933512

    DELETE chapters, sections, paragraphs
    FROM      chapters
    LEFT JOIN sections   ON   sections.subject_id = $subject_id AND   sections.chapter_id = $node
    LEFT JOIN paragraphs ON paragraphs.subject_id = $subject_id AND paragraphs.chapter_id = $node
    WHERE                     chapters.subject_id = $subject_id AND chapters.id           = $node

I'm not sure if using left joins is really faster than using 3 separate deletes.

Q: what's a good functional language for someone coming from perl? A:

I recently discovered "Janet", a programming language in the Lisp-family. It's meant to be a light-weight scripting language, which might appeal to you if you're coming from Perl.

Official home page: https://janet-lang.org/ (You can find plenty of documentation here.)

One way it differs from a lot of other Lips is that its variable scoping rules are closer to C/C++/Java/Perl than most Lisps. You might appreciate that.

Keep in mind that Janet is a little-known language. While there is plenty of documentation and a nice user community, many programmers are unaware of it.

Personally, I enjoy programming in Janet a lot. I recommend at least looking into it.
